title: Gullwind Inc - Concurrency & Streaming Bakeoff (Discovery)
summary: Discovery call to map Gullwind's peak concurrency and streaming token/sec requirements, evaluate hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs, and agree success criteria for a short pilot bakeoff. Key concerns: p95 latency targets for interactive streaming (<=200ms token), steady-state token/sec per-region, KV cache warmup, and compliance (SOC 2 / KMS).
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs
next_steps: Samira to share Redwood throughput/streaming benchmark template and cost model (by 2027-11-03)
Omar to propose pilot infra config (hosted vs dedicated) and target test plan (by 2027-11-05)
Gullwind to provide sample prompt set and expected concurrency profile (by 2027-11-04)
Schedule pilot kickoff call for week of 2027-11-08
action_items: Samira Patel: email SOC 2 and KMS integration docs plus pricing grid (2027-11-03)
Omar Ruiz: draft pilot topology w/ autoscale and KV cache settings (2027-11-05)
Priya Singh (Gullwind): upload representative prompt traces and p95 SLOs (2027-11-04)
Marcus Hale (Gullwind): provide network egress constraints and region preference (2027-11-04)
transcript:
[00:00] Samira Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Samira from Redwood, AE on this account. Omar and Li are with me from SEs. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Elena Martinez: Good, thanks. We just finished an exec sync so we're on time.
[00:12] Jon Park: Hi, Jon here. I'll be leading the perf side.
[00:15] Omar Ruiz: Great, quick agenda: understand your latency & throughput targets, current infra, and then map a pilot bakeoff. Does that sound right?
[00:22] Elena Martinez: Yep. We run an agent assistant in our product that streams token-by-token, interactive. Our big worry is p95 token latency needs to be below 200 milliseconds in our EU region and under 250ms in APAC.
[00:34] Priya Singh: For context, typical session is 60-120 tokens but sometimes we get bursts to 2k when users paste long prompts.
[00:39] Marcus Hale: We need to maintain concurrency of 500 steady users in peak windows, with bursts up to 2k concurrent requests for 3-7 minute windows during promotions.
[00:49] Li Chen: Thanks, that helps. Do you currently quantize models or use KV caching?
[00:53] Jon Park: We use off-the-shelf LLMs via another provider now; no KV cache implemented yet — we've been doing ephemeral in-memory context per request.
[01:00] Omar Ruiz: Understood. So two architectural levers matter: streaming path latency (per-token) and backend throughput (tokens/sec) plus cache warmup. We typically recommend prefix KV caching for applications like yours to reduce p95 on repeat prompts.
[01:12] Elena Martinez: Can you explain how Redwood handles KV cache warmup? We care about cold starts during those burst windows.
[01:18] Li Chen: Sure — on Dedicated and Private, you can pin model shards to a node and persist KV cache across sessions. On Hosted we use fast ephemeral caches and warmup strategies; there is a warm window cost tradeoff. For bursts, Dedicated with reserved capacity gives more predictable p95.
[01:32] Jon Park: And for hosted, do you support region pinning? We need EU primary for GDPR considerations.
[01:37] Omar Ruiz: Yes — Hosted API supports region routing; Dedicated and Private let you control exactly which region. For EU data residency we can keep inference in eu-west and support customer-managed keys via KMS in Private.
[01:47] Priya Singh: Security is big. SOC two is a checkbox for us, and we need KMS + audit logs.
[01:52] Samira Patel: We have SOC 2 Type II reports and an integration guide for KMS. I'll send the pack after the call.
[01:58] Marcus Hale: Back to perf — what's a realistic tokens/sec per GPU for the 8B-ish model we want to run?
[02:05] Omar Ruiz: It varies with quantization and sequence length. For fp16 8B on A100-class hardware, steady-state you might see ~500-1500 tokens/sec per GPU depending on batching and streaming optimizations. With q4_0 or q5 quant you can push that higher but watch quality.
[02:20] Jon Park: That range is wide. For our numbers, assuming average 80 tokens/session and 500 concurrent steady users, that's 40k tokens/sec — Is that feasible?
[02:29] Li Chen: 40k tokens/sec distributed across a pool is feasible with Dedicated reserved nodes and autoscale. The pilot would establish how many GPUs and what batch sizes to hit your p95.
[02:37] Elena Martinez: What's typical p95 per-token on your streaming pipeline? We saw numbers in a benchmark doc but curious about real-world.
[02:44] Omar Ruiz: In our hosted benchmarks, p95 per-token latency for streaming on tuned models is often 120-220ms depending on seq length and batch. When people under-provision or lack caching, that climbs. Key is tail behavior — consistent queuing discipline and fallback policies.
[02:57] Jon Park: Do fallbacks mean returning shorter outputs or switching to smaller model?
[03:01] Li Chen: Exactly — automatic fallback to a smaller variant or a cached answer to keep UI responsive. We can set policy thresholds by latency or queue depth.
[03:09] Priya Singh: For the burst windows, are there options for temporary burst capacity? We don't want to pay for 2k steady GPUs.
[03:15] Omar Ruiz: Yes — Dedicated has burst pools and hosted has elastic tiers; both can spike for a short window. There's a cost vs SLO tradeoff. We'll show modeled costs in the pilot pricing template.
[03:26] Elena Martinez: We're evaluating three paths: keep current provider, move to Redwood Hosted for speed of adoption, or Redwood Dedicated/Private for predictability and data controls.
[03:34] Samira Patel: Makes sense. For a bakeoff, we recommend a short 2-week pilot: Week 1 benchmarking in your staging with our hosted config, Week 2 run dedicated nodes to compare p95 and cost. Pilot test plan will include streaming latency traces, token/sec ramp tests, and KV cache cold-start scenarios.
[03:51] Jon Park: For the token/sec ramp tests, can you share a script or harness?
[03:55] Omar Ruiz: We'll share a benchmark harness that replays recorded prompt traces at scale and measures per-token latency, p95, p99, and drop rates. It also simulates KV cache hit rates.
[04:05] Marcus Hale: Are there network egress issues we should plan for? Our infra team wants to limit cross-region egress and inspect TLS flows.
[04:12] Li Chen: We can run the pilot inside your VPC for Private or use peering for Dedicated; hosted region routing keeps data inside region but egress to Redwood's control plane exists unless you choose private deployment.
[04:23] Elena Martinez: Cost question: what's the unit cost for streaming tokens on hosted? We're trying to budget for the pilot budget cap of $20k.
[04:31] Samira Patel: I'll send a sample cost model. For a rough estimate, streaming tends to be priced per token with tiering, plus instance-hour costs if you pin dedicated GPUs. We'll work within your $20k pilot budget in the proposal.
[04:44] Jon Park: In terms of SLO measurement, we care about p95 token latency during steady-state and during a 5-minute sustained burst. Can you capture both?
[04:50] Omar Ruiz: Yes — pilot harness will report sliding-window p95s and tail-latency under burst load. We'll also measure cold-start percents for KV cache and include recommendations to mitigate.
[04:59] Elena Martinez: Any gotchas with streaming and function/tool calling? We use tool-calls to fetch internal data mid-stream.
[05:05] Li Chen: Tool-calls add latencies because of synchronous calls out to your services; common pattern is to prefetch or make the tool-call asynchronous with optimistic UI. We can instrument traces to understand where time is spent.
[05:16] Jon Park: For the payloads, average context length 512 tokens — how does that affect throughput?
[05:21] Omar Ruiz: Longer context increases compute per token due to attention costs; throughput per GPU drops as sequence grows. We'll include sequence-length specific profiles in the benchmark.
[05:31] Marcus Hale: Is there support for on-prem? Some regulators in our vertical ask for air-gapped options for certain data.
[05:37] Samira Patel: Yes — Redwood Private can be deployed in customer VPCs or on-prem with HSM/KMS integration; there is an enterprise package and professional services.
[05:46] Elena Martinez: Ok good. Let's talk about acceptance criteria: p95 token latency <=200ms in EU during steady-state at 500 concurrency with KV cache enabled, p95 during 5-minute bursts <=350ms, and cost below X (TBD after your model). If we hit those, we move to a quarter-long reserved Dedicated setup.
[06:06] Omar Ruiz: Clear. We'll codify those in the pilot success metrics.
[06:10] Jon Park: One more technical — how does Redwood handle KV cache eviction across nodes? We try to avoid cache fragmentation across a big pool.
[06:17] Li Chen: Eviction is LRU-based per-shard; on Dedicated you can pin users to shards to increase locality. We also offer sticky routing so requests from same session go to same shard while the session is warm.
[06:29] Priya Singh: Does sticky routing increase tail risk if a node fails?
[06:33] Omar Ruiz: There's a tradeoff — sticky routing improves p95 for warm sessions but requires good fallback and replication policies to handle node failures. We include replication suggestions in the pilot topology.
[06:45] Elena Martinez: For the pilot, we'd prefer Redwood to run the hosted test first so we can iterate quickly; then switch to a dedicated config if the numbers look promising.
[06:54] Samira Patel: That's our usual pattern. We'll put together a hosted-first pilot plan.
[06:59] Marcus Hale: About observability — we need token-level traces, per-route latency, and alerting hooks.
[07:05] Li Chen: Redwood Console exposes token-level cost and latency, per-route dashboards, and can forward traces to your Datadog/Prometheus. We'll include webhook alerts for p95 regressions.
[07:15] Jon Park: Good. Any examples of similar customers? We saw case studies but curious if there's one with similar concurrency and streaming needs.
[07:21] Samira Patel: We have a media client with similar streaming loads; I'll include an anonymized perf snapshot in the follow-up.
[07:27] Elena Martinez: Great. On timeline, we want the pilot to start by 2027-11-15. Is that doable?
[07:33] Samira Patel: Yes; if we get the prompt traces and region constraints by 2027-11-04 we can start the hosted benchmark on the 15th.
[07:40] Jon Park: For evaluation metrics, include p95 daytime vs nighttime, p99, and tokens-per-second baseline.
[07:46] Omar Ruiz: Will do. Also we'll include a short regression test for hallucination rates if you want, though that's more model-level than infra.
[07:53] Priya Singh: We might run two model sizes in parallel to compare quality vs cost.
[07:57] Li Chen: That's a good idea — pilot can include A/B across model variants with the same prompt set.
[08:03] Elena Martinez: Alright, sounds like a plan. Any blockers on your side?
[08:07] Samira Patel: We just need the traces and a point of contact for infra. Also permission to run tests from your test VPC if you choose Private.
[08:15] Marcus Hale: We'll coordinate. I'll be the infra lead for the pilot.
[08:18] Jon Park: One last question — how do you measure end-to-end from client to token emission? We want to correlate client-perceived time with server metrics.
[08:25] Omar Ruiz: We'll instrument with traces that annotate client send time, queue time, generation time per token, and network time. That lets you map client p95 to server-side bottlenecks.
[08:36] Samira Patel: I'll attach the instrumented benchmark repo and a short README.
[08:39] Elena Martinez: Perfect. If there's nothing else, let's recap next steps.
[08:43] Samira Patel: Recap: Samira send SOC 2/KMS and pricing, Omar sends pilot topology + harness, Gullwind provides traces + region/constraints, schedule kickoff for week of 11/15.
[08:54] Jon Park: Confirmed.
[08:55] Priya Singh: We'll aim to have traces by the 4th.
[08:57] Marcus Hale: I'll confirm VPC peering options.
[09:00] Samira Patel: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with calendar invites and the pilot docs.
[09:04] Elena Martinez: Thanks all.
[09:06] (call ends)

Notes on transcript quality: some product names transcribed slightly off (e.g., \"Redwood Dedicated\" heard as \"Dedicate\" in one spot). Occasional crosstalk and filler words retained.
